#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS)
Description: The Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS) has collected data since 1991 on Medicare beneficiaries' social and medical risk factors and the relationship between these factors, healthcare utilization, and health outcomes – at a point in time and over time - directly from beneficiaries. These data, linked with Medicare enrollment data and claims, provide information not otherwise available through administrative data on the Medicare program and can be used to evaluate effectiveness of health care policy and policy interventions.
URL: https://cms.gov/data-research/research/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

(a) Health care of the aged and disabled

The Secretary shall carry on studies and develop recommendations to be submitted from time to time to the Congress relating to health care of the aged and the disabled, including studies and recommendations concerning (1) the adequacy of existing personnel and facilities for health care for purposes of the programs under parts A and B of this subchapter; (2) methods for encouraging the further development of efficient and economical forms of health care which are a constructive alternative to inpatient hospital care; and (3) the effects of the deductibles and coinsurance provisions upon beneficiaries, persons who provide health services, and the financing of the program.

(b) Operation and administration of insurance programs

The Secretary shall make a continuing study of the operation and administration of this subchapter (including a validation of the accreditation process of national accreditation bodies under section 1395bb(a) of this title [1] the operation and administration of health maintenance organizations authorized by section 226 of the Social Security Amendments of 1972 [42 U.S.C. 1395mm], the experiments and demonstration projects authorized by section 402 of the Social Security Amendments of 1967 [42 U.S.C. 1395b–1] and the experiments and demonstration projects authorized by section 222(a) of the Social Security Amendments of 1972 [42 U.S.C. 1395b–1 note]), and shall transmit to the Congress annually a report concerning the operation of such programs.

(Aug. 14, 1935, ch. 531, title XVIII, § 1875, as added Pub. L. 89–97, title I, § 102(a), July 30, 1965, 79 Stat. 332; amended Pub. L. 90–248, title IV, § 402(c), Jan. 2, 1968, 81 Stat. 931; Pub. L. 110–275, title I, § 125(b)(4), July 15, 2008, 122 Stat. 2519.)

Editorial Notes
References in Text

Section 226 of the Social Security Amendments of 1972, referred to in subsec. (b), is section 226 of Pub. L. 92–603, which enacted section 1395mm of this title and provisions set out as notes under that section and amended this section and sections 1395f, 1395l, and 1396b of this title.

Section 402 of the Social Security Amendments of 1967, referred to in subsec. (b), is section 402 of Pub. L. 90–248, which enacted section 1395b–1 of this title and amended this section.

Section 222(a) of the Social Security Amendments of 1972, referred to in subsec. (b), is section 222(a) of Pub. L. 92–603, which enacted provisions set out as note under section 1395b–1 of this title.

Amendments

2008—Subsec. (b). Pub. L. 110–275 substituted “national accreditation bodies under section 1395bb(a) of this title” for “the Joint Commission on Accreditation of Hospitals,”.

2003—Subsec. (b). Pub. L. 108–173 substituted “this subchapter” for “the insurance programs under parts A and B of this subchapter”.

Subsec. (c)(7). Pub. L. 101–234, § 301(b)(5), (d)(2), amended par. (7) identically, substituting “date of the enactment of this section” for “date of the enactment of this Act”.

1988—Subsec. (c)(3). Pub. L. 100–647 amended par. (3) generally. Prior to amendment, par. (3) read as follows: “For purposes of carrying out the research program, there are authorized to be appropriated—

“(A) from the Federal Hospital Insurance Trust Fund $4,000,000 for fiscal year 1987 and $5,000,000 for each of fiscal years 1988 and 1989, and

Institute of Medicine Evaluation and Report on Health Care Performance Measures

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS)
Description: The Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS) has collected data since 1991 on Medicare beneficiaries' social and medical risk factors and the relationship between these factors, healthcare utilization, and health outcomes – at a point in time and over time - directly from beneficiaries. These data, linked with Medicare enrollment data and claims, provide information not otherwise available through administrative data on the Medicare program and can be used to evaluate effectiveness of health care policy and policy interventions.
URL: https://cms.gov/data-research/research/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS): Research and Preservation Report

**Research date:** October 9, 2026  
**Federal publisher:** Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)  
**Official landing page:** [Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey](https://www.cms.gov/data-research/research/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey)

## Executive assessment

**Your title, description, and URL are substantially correct.** The description closely matches CMS’s own overview. MCBS began in 1991 and combines interviews with Medicare administrative records to study beneficiaries’ health, circumstances, insurance, access to care, utilization, and expenditures.

Three qualifications are essential:

1. **MCBS is a survey program and family of data products, not one flat dataset.** Public-use files, limited-access files, cost supplements, early releases, and historical products differ materially.
2. **Continuous collection does not mean an uninterrupted published annual series.** CMS did not release 2014 MCBS data.
3. **“Nationally representative” needs a year-specific geographic definition.** Before the 2026 redesign, the sampling frame excluded Alaska and Hawaii; Puerto Rico was removed in 2017. A redesign starting with the Fall 2026 incoming panel expands sampling to all 50 states and Washington, D.C., with state-level estimation intended after full implementation in 2029.

**Why preserve it:** MCBS records experiences that Medicare claims cannot adequately capture—unmet need, affordability, disability and functioning, satisfaction, supplemental insurance, and care paid for outside Medicare. Its linked survey–administrative structure makes it unusually valuable for evaluating how a major public insurance program affects people, rather than merely documenting what the program paid for.

Sources: [CMS overview](https://www.cms.gov/data-research/research/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey), [CMS ordering page](https://www.cms.gov/data-research/files-for-order/limited-data-set-lds-files/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey-mcbs), [2026 sampling supporting statement](https://omb.report/icr/202607-0938-013/doc/171257300.pdf).

---

## 1. Identity and institutional responsibility

| Attribute | Finding |
|---|---|
| Official name | Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey |
| Acronym | MCBS |
| Responsible federal agency | CMS, within HHS |
| Sponsoring office | CMS Office of Enterprise Data and Analytics (OEDA) |
| Current survey contractor | NORC at the University of Chicago |
| Beginning of collection | 1991 |
| Nature of resource | Repeated interviews with rotating panels, linked to administrative records |
| Principal statistical subjects | Medicare beneficiaries and their health-care experiences |
| Principal distribution sites | CMS.gov for program information and documentation; data.CMS.gov for public-use products; CMS’s limited-data-set request process for restricted products |
| Main research contact | **MCBS@cms.hhs.gov** |
| OMB control number | **0938-0568** |
| Information-collection title | Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS), CMS-P-0015A |

CMS is the authoritative publisher and federal steward. NORC conducts sampling, interviewing, processing, editing, imputation, and delivery to CMS for final processing and dissemination. NORC’s project dates are **2014–present**; that is the contractor’s tenure, not the survey’s inception.

The survey began under CMS’s predecessor, the Health Care Financing Administration. Organizational names and offices in older documentation therefore differ from current ones.

Sources: [CMS overview](https://www.cms.gov/data-research/research/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey), [NORC project description](https://www.norc.org/research/projects/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey.html), [2014 contractor announcement](https://www.norc.org/research/library/norc-at-the-university-of-chicago-selected-by-centers-for-medica.html).

## 2. Legal authority, mandate, and oversight

### Statutory authority

CMS identifies **section 1875 of the Social Security Act, codified at 42 U.S.C. § 1395ll**, as MCBS’s authority.

The statutory citation ends in **two lowercase letters “l”**, not the digits “11,” although some CMS/HHS page renderings make this ambiguous.

The statute directs the HHS Secretary to:

- Study health care for aged and disabled people and develop recommendations for Congress.
- Examine matters including health-care resources, efficient alternatives to inpatient care, and the effects of deductibles and coinsurance.
- Conduct continuing studies of Medicare’s operation and administration.
- Report annually to Congress concerning the operation of the covered programs.

**Important distinction:** This is a broad statutory research and reporting mandate. It does not specify MCBS by name or guarantee that a particular questionnaire, release format, or collection schedule must continue indefinitely.

Source: [42 U.S.C. § 1395ll—Studies and recommendations](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/1395ll).

### Paperwork Reduction Act oversight

MCBS is subject to Office of Management and Budget review under control number **0938-0568**.

The approval record for the revision submitted in November 2025 shows:

- Approval on **January 6, 2026**.
- An approved expiration date of **January 31, 2029**, also shown on NORC’s participant website.
- Terms requiring assessment of respondent burden before subsequent resubmission.

A further revision submitted **July 27, 2026** was displayed as **“Received in OIRA”** in the reviewed record. Its proposed changes should not be treated as approved merely because they appear in supporting documents.

Sources: [Approved 2025-submitted collection](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202511-0938-005), [July 2026 revision](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202607-0938-013), [NORC participant information](https://mcbs.norc.org/what-is-the-mcbs.html).

### Voluntary participation and confidentiality

Participation is voluntary. CMS/NORC materials state that participation decisions do not affect respondents’ relationship with CMS programs.

The 2026 supporting statement identifies:

- Privacy Act protections.
- A system of records, **09-70-0519**.
- A modified system-of-records notice published February 14, 2018, at **83 FR 6591**.
- Confidentiality training and security procedures.
- Research and statistical uses of responses.
- Specific HIPAA explanations for participating facilities.

The assurance is that information is kept private **“to the extent permitted by law.”** It should not be paraphrased as an absolute guarantee of confidentiality under every circumstance.

Source: [2026 supporting statement A](https://omb.report/icr/202607-0938-013/doc/171257400.pdf).

| Period | Development and significance |

| **1992** | Historical Cost and Use series begins. |
| **1991–2013** | Principal releases use the Access to Care and Cost and Use structure. Older files use Record Identification Code structures. |
| **2014** | NORC assumes the survey contract. Sampling and collection transition occurs. **2014 data are not released.** |

| **2016** | First public-use files are released, initially using 2013 data. CMS’s Office of Minority Health supported their development to expand health-disparities research. |

| **2020–2021** | COVID-19 supplements document pandemic experiences; public-use versions are available. |
| **December 10, 2024** | MCBS microdata public-use files move to **data.CMS.gov**. |
| **Recent releases** | Early-release Survey Files provide selected Fall-round information on an expedited schedule. |
| **Fall 2026–2029** | New state-stratified, nationwide sample is phased in through successive incoming panels. |

The **2014 gap is a substantive limitation**, not a broken download link. CMS explicitly warns that an annual cost/utilization analysis covering 2013–2015 cannot simply include an unpublished 2014 year.

Sources: [CMS historical FAQ](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/2019-mcbs-data-user-frequently-asked-questions.pdf), [historical-file explanation](https://resdac.org/articles/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey-mcbs-differences-between-cost-and-use-and-access-care), [year-to-year comparison tutorial](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/mcbs-advanced-tutorial-year-year-estimate-comparisons.pdf), [announcements](https://www.cms.gov/data-research/research/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey-mcbs/announcements).

## 4. Population, sampling, and collection

### Population represented

Depending on the file and year, MCBS covers:

- Beneficiaries aged 65 and older.
- Beneficiaries under 65 who qualify for Medicare.
- Traditional fee-for-service Medicare and Medicare Advantage enrollees.
- Medicare–Medicaid dual-eligible beneficiaries.
- Community residents and long-term-care facility residents.
- Newly enrolled beneficiaries and people who die during a reference year.

**Not every released file includes every population.** In particular, CMS describes Survey File public-use products as covering community-dwelling beneficiaries only.

### Rotating panels

MCBS follows sampled people rather than interviewing an entirely new sample each year:

- A new panel enters each Fall.
- Participants can be interviewed up to three times annually.
- A panel remains for approximately four years.
- The established schedule includes up to **11 interviews**.
- Cross-sectional releases combine overlapping panels.

Thus, it supports both population snapshots and longitudinal analysis, but it is **not a lifelong cohort**.

### Interview sources and modes

Collection includes community and facility components:

- Community information comes from beneficiaries or proxy respondents when appropriate.
- Facility information comes through facility respondents and records; it is not uniformly a direct interview with the resident.
- Interviews use phone and in-person modes.
- Respondents are encouraged to retain bills, statements, and calendars to support reporting of services and payments.

Your phrase “directly from beneficiaries” accurately describes the survey’s purpose, but should be qualified to acknowledge proxies and facility sources.

### Geographic redesign

Before the new design, MCBS used a multistage clustered sample involving primary and secondary sampling units. The 2026 supporting statement explains that this design supported national—not representative state-level—estimation.

Starting with the Fall 2026 incoming panel:

- The frame covers all **50 states and D.C.**
- Sampling is stratified by state and three age groups: under 65, 65–79, and 80+.
- Ethnicity is no longer an additional stratification dimension.
- The redesign is intended to support state and subnational estimates after four-year implementation.

**Do not assume a state estimate is valid simply because a restricted file contains geographic information.** Likewise, approval of the redesign does not make earlier files state-representative.

Sources: [MCBS methodology report](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/mcbs-methodology-report.pdf), [2026 sampling supporting statement](https://omb.report/icr/202607-0938-013/doc/171257300.pdf), [CMS introductory tutorial](https://www.cms.gov/Research-Statistics-Data-and-Systems/Research/MCBS/Downloads/MCBS_Tutorial.pdf).

## 5. What the data contain

The Survey File LDS contains **more than 6,000 variables**, according to CMS. Content changes across years and rounds.

| Domain | Examples of information |
|---|---|
| Demographic and socioeconomic circumstances | Age, race/ethnicity, education, income-related information, household and housing characteristics |
| Health | Self-reported health, chronic conditions, disability, cognitive and functional status |
| Access and experience | Usual source of care, difficulty obtaining care, delayed or forgone care, satisfaction |
| Insurance | Medicare enrollment, Medicare Advantage, supplemental coverage, Medicaid, prescription coverage |
| Behavior and prevention | Preventive care, screenings, behavioral risk factors, medication non-adherence |
| Utilization | Hospital, outpatient, physician/provider, dental, prescription medicine, facility, and other services |
| Spending | Expenditures, out-of-pocket payments, and sources of payment |
| Knowledge and engagement | Knowledge of Medicare, attitudes, engagement and activation |
| Special topics | Pandemic experiences and other rotating policy-relevant questionnaire sections |

### Administrative linkage

CMS describes the full Survey File as augmented with:

- **Five years of enrollment data**.
- **Five years of limited fee-for-service claims** for FFS beneficiaries.

The Cost Supplement combines survey-reported events and administrative information to provide utilization, expenditure, and payer information, including services not covered by Medicare.

Facility processing can draw on other CMS administrative sources, including Minimum Data Set information.

**Claims linkage is not uniform across enrollment types.** FFS claims availability should not be generalized to an equivalent complete claims history for Medicare Advantage beneficiaries.

Source: [CMS overview and product descriptions](https://www.cms.gov/data-research/research/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey).

## 7. Formats, identifiers, metadata, and documentation

### Formats

Public-use documentation describes:

- CSV files.
- SAS export files.
- SAS import programs, formats, and labels.
- Codebooks and Data User’s Guides.
- Survey segments organized by collection season in some releases.

A technical trap: documented files with an **`.xpt` extension** are read using **SAS `PROC CIMPORT`**. Do not assume that every generic XPORT reader in R or Python will import them correctly. CSV is often the simpler route, provided that labels and special missing values are reconstructed from documentation.

Sources: [Survey PUF guide](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/2021-mcbs-puf-data-user-guide.pdf), [Cost Supplement PUF guide](https://data.cms.gov/sites/default/files/2025-01/CSPUF2022_DUG.pdf).

### Identifiers and linkage

Historical restricted products use **BASEID** to link beneficiary records. Public-use files have their own identifiers.

Do not assume:

- Public identifiers equal restricted identifiers.
- Identifiers remain linkable across all public-use years.
- Every product can be joined to every other product.
- Identical variable names guarantee identical definitions.

Check the specific release guide before designing longitudinal joins.

### Essential documentation

CMS provides:

- Data User’s Guides.
- Codebooks and file descriptions.
- Questionnaire specifications and documentation.
- Methodology reports.
- Release notes.
- Variable crosswalks.
- FAQs.
- Tutorials on weighting, longitudinal analysis, pooled cross-sections, facilities, and year-to-year comparisons.

The crosswalks show variable presence across years; CMS explicitly says they should be used **with**, not instead of, detailed documentation.

Official index: [Data Documentation and Codebooks](https://www.cms.gov/data-research/research/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey/data-documentation-codebooks).

## 8. Statistical use and analytical limitations

MCBS’s richness does not eliminate survey-design or measurement problems.

### Required analytical practices

1. **Choose the correct population and weight.**  
   Cross-sectional, longitudinal, Fall-round, and other topic-specific weights may target different populations.

2. **Account for the sample design in uncertainty estimates.**  
   MCBS supplies replicate weights and design information. Unweighted analyses or ordinary independent-observation standard errors can be misleading.

3. **Treat repeated observations as dependent.**  
   Annual files include overlapping panels. Pooling them does not create an independent sample of unique people.

4. **Distinguish “ever enrolled” from “continuously enrolled.”**  
   This matters particularly for mortality, new enrollment, and annual expenditures. Historical Access to Care and Cost and Use products targeted different populations.

5. **Preserve missingness distinctions.**  
   Refusal, “don’t know,” structural skips, unavailable information, and imputed values are not interchangeable. PUF recoding sometimes combines distinctions available in restricted data.

6. **Audit imputation and survey–claims reconciliation.**  
   Cost estimates are processed statistical products, not merely a sum of raw beneficiary recollections.

7. **Check modes and questionnaire changes.**  
   CMS publishes a working paper on data-quality effects of the transition from in-person to phone collection.

8. **Evaluate small-domain precision.**  
   National representativeness does not assure reliable estimates for rare conditions, small racial/ethnic groups, or fine geographic subdivisions.

### Additional limits

- **Recall and reporting error:** calendars and frequent interviews help, but do not eliminate it.
- **Nonresponse and attrition:** weighting addresses these imperfectly; examine year-specific response documentation.
- **Proxy effects:** proxy reports can differ from self-reports.
- **PUF disclosure protection:** recoding, aggregation, and omitted variables limit detail.
- **Release lag:** full expenditure products arrive later than interviews.
- **2014 gap and redesigns:** long time-series comparisons require harmonization.
- **Observational design:** MCBS can support policy evaluation, but causal claims require a defensible identification strategy.
- **No automatic local representativeness:** older files do not support representative state estimates simply because they contain locations.

Sources: [Weighting tutorial](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/mcbs-advanced-tutorial-weighting-and-variance-estimation.pdf), [methodology report](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/mcbs-methodology-report.pdf), [historical product populations](https://resdac.org/articles/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey-mcbs-differences-between-cost-and-use-and-access-care), [documentation index](https://www.cms.gov/data-research/research/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey/data-documentation-codebooks).

## 9. Typical users and demonstrated uses

### Federal policy and budget users

CMS uses MCBS to administer, monitor, and evaluate Medicare.

NORC’s 2014 contract announcement specifically identifies uses in products from:

- The **Congressional Budget Office**.
- The **Medicare Payment Advisory Commission**.

It also describes an intended role in monitoring Affordable Care Act provisions and new care-delivery and coordination models.

NORC’s participant materials state that MCBS informed Medicare enhancements, including development of the **Part D prescription drug benefit**. This is an institutional account of contribution—not evidence that MCBS alone caused the legislation.

### Researchers

The principal research communities include:

- Health-services researchers and health economists.
- Gerontology, disability, and long-term-care researchers.
- Epidemiologists and population-health scientists.
- Insurance and pharmaceutical-policy analysts.
- Researchers studying disparities, social circumstances, and financial burden.

CMS’s introductory tutorial identifies applications such as payment reforms, caregiver burden, prevention, supplemental insurance, behavioral risks, out-of-pocket spending, and pandemic experiences.

### Public-interest users

Public-use files make the data useful to:

- Advocacy organizations.
- Journalists and policy analysts.
- Teaching programs and students.
- Libraries providing research support.
- Community organizations interested in older people and disabled beneficiaries.

These are practical user groups enabled by public access; this report does not claim that every organization in those categories has used MCBS.

Sources: [NORC contract announcement](https://www.norc.org/research/library/norc-at-the-university-of-chicago-selected-by-centers-for-medica.html), [participant overview](https://mcbs.norc.org/what-is-the-mcbs.html), [CMS research tutorial](https://www.cms.gov/Research-Statistics-Data-and-Systems/Research/MCBS/Downloads/MCBS_Tutorial.pdf).

## 10. Benefits to the public

### Makes unmet need visible

Claims reveal services billed or paid for. They generally cannot show that someone avoided treatment because of cost, transportation, or other barriers. MCBS helps document that missing part of the story.

### Measures household financial burden

Medicare payments are not the same as beneficiaries’ total spending. MCBS includes other payers and services outside Medicare coverage, supporting affordability analysis.

### Connects social circumstances with health-care experiences

Survey information allows analysis of income, functioning, housing, and other circumstances alongside utilization and health.

### Supports scrutiny of insurance and benefit policy

It can help examine supplemental coverage, prescription benefits, cost-sharing, Medicare Advantage, and delivery-system reforms—subject to appropriate design and comparability safeguards.

### Expands independent research

Free PUFs allow research without buying restricted data or negotiating a DUA. CMS’s Office of Minority Health explicitly supported public-use development to improve access for disparities research.

### Creates a historical record

MCBS documents how beneficiaries experienced Medicare across changes in benefits, enrollment, care delivery, and public-health emergencies.

**Public value is not equivalent to proven benefit from every release.** The defensible claim is that MCBS supplies otherwise unavailable evidence used in research and policymaking.

Source: [CMS Office of Minority Health account of PUF development](https://www.cms.gov/priorities/health-equity/minority-health/research-data/current-beneficiary-survey-public-use-file).

## 11. Funding and continuity considerations

The July 2026 supporting statement estimates:

- **$22.3 million** for contractor survey development, operations, processing, and analysis for May 1, 2026–April 30, 2027.
- Approximately **$2.14 million** in CMS staff costs.

These are **planning estimates**, not audited expenditures or a permanent appropriation.

Continuity depends on contracting, funding, approval, participation, and technical infrastructure. The 2014 transition illustrates that collection, processing, and public release can diverge.

The proposed 2027 revision also describes questionnaire changes intended to reduce burden. Preservationists should retain the proposals, approvals, and final questionnaires: removed questions can alter the evidentiary record even if the survey continues.

Source: [2026 supporting statement A](https://omb.report/icr/202607-0938-013/doc/171257400.pdf).

## 12. Preservation priorities

**Preserve the data together with the information needed to interpret them.** A CSV without weights, labels, and eligibility rules is an incomplete research object.

### Recommended preservation package

For each public release, retain:

- Original compressed download packages and extracted files.
- Every supplied format, including CSV and SAS files.
- Import scripts, formats, and labels.
- Codebooks and Data User’s Guides.
- Release notes and corrections.
- Questionnaires and specifications.
- Applicable methodology reports.
- Variable crosswalks.
- Relevant announcements and landing-page snapshots.
- Download URLs, retrieval dates, file sizes, and cryptographic checksums.
- A manifest identifying data year, release date, product, access tier, version, and population.

Retain OMB collection packages and system-of-records notices as governance context.

### Dataset-specific risks

| Risk | Preservation response |
|---|---|
| Website migration and redirects | Preserve both old and new URLs; retain page snapshots and download manifests. |
| Historical naming changes | Catalog Access to Care, Cost and Use, Survey File, and Cost Supplement as related but distinct series. |
| Proprietary or unusual SAS formats | Keep originals plus validated open-format derivatives. |
| Metadata dispersed across sites | Create a local documentation bundle for each release. |
| Missing 2014 release | Record it explicitly; do not silently interpolate. |
| Geographic redesign | Preserve frame, weighting, and implementation documentation. |
| Revisions to questionnaires | Retain each questionnaire version and its effective rounds. |
| Public/restricted confusion | Label access tiers prominently and segregate storage. |

### Restricted-data preservation

An institution’s DUA governs its restricted files. **Do not place LDS data in an open repository or treat an expired project copy as an unrestricted archival asset.** Retention, destruction, transfer, and disclosure obligations must be checked against the agreement.

I did **not** establish a dataset-specific NARA disposition rule or a guaranteed permanent preservation arrangement for every MCBS product. Those remain useful follow-up questions for CMS’s records-management and MCBS offices.

## 13. Cataloging recommendations for data librarians

Catalog MCBS hierarchically:

**Program → product family → data year → access tier → release/version**

A recommended record should include:

- Corporate creator: CMS.
- Sponsor: OEDA.
- Collector/processor: NORC, with applicable dates.
- Official product title and historical aliases.
- Data reference year versus actual publication date.
- Coverage geography and eligibility population.
- Community/facility inclusion.
- Sampling design and panel structure.
- Administrative-linkage coverage.
- File formats and documentation dependencies.
- Access conditions and DUA requirements.
- Version and retrieval date.
- Known discontinuities.

**Do not equate a CMS page’s “Publish Year” field with the actual release date.** Preserve dated announcements as separate provenance evidence.

Suggested citation template:

> Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. *Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey, [product], [data year], [PUF/LDS], [version or release date].* [URL]. Accessed [date].

This is a librarian-oriented template, not a verified CMS-mandated citation format. Follow release-specific acknowledgment instructions where provided.

## 14. Practical guidance for data scientists and policy activists

### For data scientists

- Start with the research population and outcome, then select the product.
- Prototype with a PUF when possible, but check whether omitted variables make the question infeasible.
- Use a documented, survey-aware analysis workflow.
- Reproduce published benchmark estimates before extending the analysis.
- Keep immutable source files and versioned transformations.
- Test joins, missing-value handling, weights, and unit-of-analysis assumptions.
- Use variable crosswalks to locate candidates, then inspect wording and eligibility.
- For policy evaluation, distinguish descriptive associations from causal effects.

### For policy activists

Strong questions include:

- Who cannot afford or obtain needed care?
- Which beneficiaries experience high out-of-pocket burdens?
- How do access and satisfaction differ by disability, income, or coverage?
- Do benefit changes reach those with the greatest needs?
- What experiences are invisible in claims-only analyses?

Publish weighted estimates with uncertainty, population definitions, and limitations. Do not portray community-only findings as representing facility residents. Avoid unsupported state comparisons from older releases.

For oversight, track questionnaire deletions, release delays, public-use availability, and the implementation of the nationwide sample redesign. OMB and Federal Register review processes are important opportunities to document proposed changes and submit evidence about their consequences.

## 15. Outstanding questions and research limitations

This report verified the program’s identity, governing authority, major history, data products, access pathways, sampling evolution, principal documentation, and institutional accounts of use.

It was **not a file-level preservation audit**. I did not download and validate every annual microdata package, reproduce estimates, or verify all scheduled releases.

Follow-up work should establish:

1. Exact currently posted versions and checksums for all public products.
2. Release-specific response rates, sample counts, and nonresponse findings.
3. Product-specific public-use linkage capabilities.
4. Explicit redistribution terms or licenses for preservation mirrors.
5. Restricted-file retention obligations.
6. NARA disposition and long-term preservation arrangements.
7. Final status of the July 2026 OMB revision.
8. Implementation details and comparability guidance for the 2026–2029 redesign.

**Overall conclusion:** MCBS merits high preservation priority. Its value lies in the linked, repeated record of beneficiaries’ experiences and costs. Preserving that value requires retaining the questionnaires, statistical design, weights, processing rules, and release history—not just the observations themselves.

**Assessment date: October 9, 2026**

## Overall finding

**The strongest documented risk is loss of content and comparability in future MCBS releases—not wholesale removal of existing files.** MCBS remains operational, has active OMB approval, and continues publishing research files. However, approved questionnaire reductions and an explicit presidential-action-linked requirement to reduce respondent burden warrant **High Risk** ratings for Data Quality and Policy under your rubric.

I found **no substantiated evidence that CMS has deleted or politically altered previously published MCBS microdata**. That conclusion is qualified: this review examined release inventories, announcements, information-collection records, and related sources—not checksums or every historical download.

### Scope and interpretation

- MCBS is a **family of products**. Free public-use files (PUFs) and restricted limited data sets (LDS) have different content and access conditions.
- I distinguish **removing information from historical releases** from **stopping collection of that information prospectively**.
- Proposed budgets and pending questionnaire changes are identified as proposals, not treated as implemented.
- “No Known Issue” means the available evidence does not establish a rubric trigger; it is not a guarantee.
- CMS’s announcements page contains an **October 30, 2026** entry despite this assessment’s October 9 retrieval date. I exclude that future-dated entry from evidence of completed releases.

- The LDS ordering page lists Survey Files for **2015–2024** and Cost Supplements for **2015–2023**.
- CMS’s December 10, 2024 migration announcement identifies historical PUFs moved to **data.CMS.gov**. This is a documented relocation, not evidence of deletion.  
  Sources: [CMS MCBS overview](https://www.cms.gov/data-research/research/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey), [LDS ordering page](https://www.cms.gov/data-research/files-for-order/limited-data-set-lds-files/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey-mcbs), [announcements](https://www.cms.gov/data-research/research/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey-mcbs/announcements).

**Moderate Risk — not established**
- Questionnaire items have been removed prospectively, but I found no evidence that CMS stripped those items from already-published historical releases.
- PUFs contain fewer variables than LDS files by design. That longstanding disclosure-protection distinction does not itself establish a recent historical alteration.

**High Risk / Gone — not established**
- I found no documented withdrawal of previously available annual MCBS files.
- **2014 data were never released**, according to CMS. This is an important historical gap, but not evidence that a previously published file was removed. [CMS explanation](https://www.cms.gov/data-research/files-for-order/limited-data-set-lds-files/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey-mcbs).

### Selected level: **No Known Issue**

Historical release inventories remain available, with no substantiated retrospective deletion or alteration. Confidence is **moderate**, because listed availability is not a file-integrity audit.

## 2. Future Data Availability

### Evidence by risk level

**No Known Issue — substantial supporting evidence**
- OMB approved the MCBS revision on **January 6, 2026**, with expiration on **January 31, 2029**.
- CMS announced the **2024 full Survey File LDS on July 6, 2026**, consistent with its summer release pattern.
- CMS announced the **2025 Early Release LDS on September 22, 2026**.
- The July 2026 revision requests continuing collection beginning Winter 2027, rather than terminating it.  
  Sources: [approved OMB record](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202511-0938-005), [CMS announcements](https://www.cms.gov/data-research/research/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey-mcbs/announcements), [pending revision](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202607-0938-013).

**Moderate Risk — limited supporting evidence**
- CMS describes Early Release data as available **within eight months of the end of Fall-round collection**. The September 22, 2026 announcement for 2025 data suggests a modest delay relative to that intended schedule.
- This is a **timeliness flag**, not a confirmed long interruption: the announcement date may not equal the first date researchers could obtain the file. [CMS schedule and product description](https://www.cms.gov/data-research/research/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey).

**High Risk — not established for the current period**
- No current skipped annual collection or publication, statutory publication-deadline violation, or year-long ICR expiration was identified.
- The unreleased 2014 cycle is a historical precedent, not evidence of a new interruption.

**Gone — not supported**
- Collection and publication continue.

### Selected level: **Moderate Risk — provisional**

The apparent Early Release slippage meets the rubric’s intended-date concern, but this is the least certain rating. Confirmation that the file was available within eight months would justify changing it to **No Known Issue**. The other principal releases and ICR show continuing operations.

---

## 3. Data Quality

### Evidence by risk level

**High Risk — supported**
- The revision approved January 6, 2026 reports **removal of 209 questionnaire items and revision of 46 items**, reducing annual respondent burden from 35,206 to 32,258 hours.
- The approval’s abstract explicitly includes items “no longer needed at the same frequency of administration.” Thus, the changes affect content and potentially measurement frequency, not merely wording. [Approved OMB record](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202511-0938-005).

**Moderate Risk — further prospective evidence**
The pending Winter 2027 revision proposes:
- Removing the 32-item Access to Care Questionnaire, while retaining and moving seven items.
- Removing detailed diabetes-management follow-ups and other health-status items.
- Removing four satisfaction-with-care items.
- Removing facility expenditure-verification and health-status items.
- Revising facility collection modes.

These changes could interrupt longstanding measures of access, chronic-disease management, and beneficiary experience. [Supporting Statement B](https://omb.report/icr/202607-0938-013/doc/171257300.pdf).

**No Known Issue — countervailing improvements**
- CMS says reductions target low-performing, outdated, or unnecessary items, using a review process developed in **2024**.
- Proposed additions cover care coordination, provider trust, prior authorization, drug-discount programs, nutrition, and hypertension management.
- The nationwide sample redesign is intended to improve geographic coverage and eventually permit state-level estimates.

These improvements may benefit response quality and new analyses, but do not restore every discontinued time series.

**Gone — not supported**
- MCBS continues.

### Selected level: **High Risk**

Approved content reductions satisfy your rubric’s granularity criterion. **This does not establish that remaining measurements are inaccurate**: burden reduction can improve survey performance. The risk is narrower coverage and weakened longitudinal comparability.

---

## 4. Statutory Context

### Evidence by risk level

**High Risk — supported**
- CMS identifies **Social Security Act §1875, 42 U.S.C. §1395ll**, as its authority.
- The statute requires Medicare studies and reporting, but does **not name MCBS**, prescribe its questionnaire, require its public-use microdata products, or establish their publication deadlines.
- Consequently, the authority provides considerable discretion over how the research obligation is fulfilled. [Statutory text](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/1395ll).

**Moderate Risk — important counterweight**
- MCBS has substantial programmatic use. The July 2026 Federal Register notice describes its role in evaluating Medicare policies, prescription-drug spending, and beneficiaries’ out-of-pocket burdens.
- CMS describes it as the only comprehensive source covering the entire spectrum of Medicare beneficiaries. Administrative records cannot fully replace beneficiary-reported access, satisfaction, or unmet need.  
  Sources: [Federal Register notice, July 24, 2026](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/24/2026-15046/agency-information-collection-activities-submission-for-omb-review-comment-request), [OMB approval abstract](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202511-0938-005).

**No Known Issue — not fully established**
- MCBS supports Medicare implementation and evaluation, but I did not find a binding requirement to maintain **this particular collection and dissemination arrangement**.

**Gone — not applicable**

### Selected level: **High Risk**

The rubric expressly treats vague authorization as a High Risk trigger. MCBS has clear research authority and important users, but lacks a dataset-specific statutory guarantee. **This is structural vulnerability, not evidence of impending cancellation.**

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

### Evidence by risk level

**No Known Issue — best-supported current classification**
- Reporting in April 2025 identified approximately **300 CMS job cuts**, below your 500-person threshold and roughly 5% of an agency with several thousand employees.
- CMS leadership reportedly said its IT team was unaffected because of the sensitivity of its datasets.
- CMS’s FY2026 operating-plan table lists total Program Management funding of **$4.125 billion in both FY2025 and FY2026**, rather than the proposed reduction.
- MCBS’s July 2026 supporting statement estimates approximately **14 CMS FTEs** and **$22.3 million** for contractor survey operations during May 2026–April 2027. These are estimates, not audited expenditure or staffing counts.  
  Sources: [CNBC reporting](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/04/04/cms-makes-job-cuts-as-rkf-jr-guts-hhs.html), [FY2026 operating plan](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/fy-2026-program-management-operating-plan.pdf), [MCBS Supporting Statement A](https://omb.report/icr/202607-0938-013/doc/171257400.pdf).

**Moderate Risk — prospective concerns**
- The FY2026 President’s Budget requested a **16.3% reduction** in comparable Program Management appropriations—from approximately $4.137 billion to $3.464 billion. That falls within your Moderate Risk budget band **if implemented**, but the operating plan does not substantiate implementation.
- Cuts affected grants/contracts administration, the minority-health office, and Medicare–Medicaid coordination—functions relevant to MCBS’s operations or research users. [Budget request](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/fy2026-cms-congressional-justification-estimates-appropriations-committees.pdf), [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/04/04/cms-makes-job-cuts-as-rkf-jr-guts-hhs.html).

**High Risk / Gone — not established for CMS/OEDA/MCBS**
- HHS-wide workforce reductions were much larger, but applying the entire department’s losses to CMS or MCBS would exaggerate the evidence.
- I found no verified MCBS/OEDA staffing loss meeting the thresholds, survey-funding termination, or removal of its leadership.

**Staffing-tracker qualification**
- The requested [USAJobs tracker](https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com) measures **job postings, not employee departures or actual hires**.
- Its notice says collection stops December 31, 2025. It cannot establish current 2026 MCBS staffing losses.

### Selected level: **No Known Issue — limited confidence**

The documented CMS cuts and enacted operating-plan funding do not establish a rubric threshold. Proposed cuts and incomplete OEDA-level staffing information justify close monitoring, but not treating an unimplemented budget request as an actual cut.

## 6. Policy

### Evidence by risk level

**High Risk — directly supported**
- OMB’s January 2026 terms require MCBS’s next burden assessment to be guided by **Executive Order 14192, “Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation.”**
- They also require offsets for additional burden from forthcoming supplemental collections.
- The July 2026 supporting statement explicitly connects further questionnaire deletions to those terms of clearance.  
  Sources: [OMB terms](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202511-0938-005), [Supporting Statement A](https://omb.report/icr/202607-0938-013/doc/171257400.pdf).

**Moderate Risk — additionally supported**
- The Winter 2027 questionnaire revision remains pending in the reviewed record.
- The Federal Register notice proposes removing multiple items and adding selected topics considered most relevant to the current health-care landscape. [Pending ICR](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202607-0938-013), [Federal Register notice](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/24/2026-15046/agency-information-collection-activities-submission-for-omb-review-comment-request).

**No Known Issue — not appropriate**
- There are documented post-January-2025 collection changes and a direct presidential-action connection.
- Nevertheless, not all reductions should be attributed to politics: CMS says its content-review process began in 2024.

**Gone — not supported**
- No termination was identified.

### Selected level: **High Risk**

The presidential-action-linked clearance terms directly meet your rubric. I found **no verified MCBS-specific instruction to purge historical race, gender, or other demographic data**; broader federal-data controversies should not be substituted for dataset-specific evidence.

## Preservation implication

Prioritize preserving **existing PUFs, questionnaires, codebooks, variable crosswalks, release notes, and OMB change packages**. The immediate concern is retaining the evidence needed to understand discontinued measures and changing time series. Preserve restricted files only as permitted by their Data Use Agreements.

Future Data Availability: **Moderate Risk**  
Data Quality: **High Risk**
